title: Chain to a synthesis
caption: The article runs as one long chain: each proposed mechanism answers a problem raised by the one before it, climbing from connectionism's failure up to a wave-based theory of consciousness, with the comparison to rival theories sitting as a side note just before the conclusion.

scenes.title: From fixed neurons to conscious waves

items.text: Cognition needs rapid coordination
items.detail: Flexible top-down thought requires coordinating hundreds of millions of neurons within fractions of a second.

items.text: Classical view: each neuron has one fixed job
items.sub: but this can't explain the data
items.detail: Hierarchical feedforward models assign each neuron a stable specialized function, but about a third of all prefrontal neurons engage in any given task.

items.text: Many neurons multiplex signals (mixed selectivity)
items.detail: A neuron may respond to an object only in one sequence position, blending identity, order, and action in one cell.

items.text: Brain waves can shift spiking directly
items.detail: Oscillating electric fields modulate nearby neurons' spiking directly, independent of synaptic connections.

items.text: Spatial Computing: alpha/beta 'stencils' gate gamma spiking
items.detail: Spatially patterned alpha/beta rhythms suppress gamma-driven spiking in some cortical spots while sparing others, routing information.

items.text: This explains mixed selectivity and low-dimensional coding
items.detail: A neuron falls inside or outside the suppressive stencil depending on context, producing context-dependent tuning without dedicated 'context neurons'.

items.text: Traveling waves shift activity between coding states
items.detail: Moving patterns of excitation and inhibition sweep across cortex and may move population activity between orthogonal coding subspaces.

items.text: Wave interference performs analog computation
items.detail: Overlapping waves add, cancel, and combine continuously, computing in parallel rather than one step at a time.

items.text: Anesthesia disrupts waves, not specific receptors
items.detail: Very different drugs all converge on the same outcome: slow, desynchronized cortical waves, suggesting consciousness tracks wave organization.

items.text: Hybrid framework: synapses store, waves control the moment
items.detail: Synaptic wiring stores long-term knowledge; wave patterns, via ephaptic feedback and analog computation, decide which representations are active right now.

items.text: Compared with Global Workspace, IIT, Higher-Order theories
items.detail: Shares themes with these theories but locates the mechanism in wave-based organization rather than broadcasting, a 'hot zone', or a separate observer.

items.text: Consciousness: an organized, wave-coordinated cortex
items.detail: Consciousness emerges when wave patterns bring the cortex into a unified, globally integrated state, built on ordinary cortical physics.

scenes.caption: A chain of steps, each one driven by a gap the previous step left open; two crowded steps are expanded in the zooms below, and a comparison to rival theories hangs off to the side near the end.

scenes.title: Why mixed selectivity needs a router

items.text: A given task engages ~1/3 of all PFC neurons
items.detail: Under a fixed-function view, the brain would saturate after learning just three tasks, so neurons must be multifunctional instead.

items.text: Neurons encode nonlinear combinations of variables
items.detail: This is called mixed selectivity: neurons blend sensory, motor, and contextual information rather than representing one thing.

items.text: E.g. a neuron fires to object A only if seen first
items.detail: The same neuron fires to object B only if it comes second, showing context-dependent, not fixed, tuning.

items.text: This hugely expands storage and computing power
items.detail: Multiplexing information across many flexible neurons stores far more than segregating it into narrow specialists.

items.text: Cortex is overlapping networks, not fixed modules
items.detail: The same neurons can take part in different computations at different times, shifting network membership as needed.

items.text: Problem: how to route signals without knowing which synapses to use
items.detail: Dynamically routing signals through a dense web of overlapping networks is hard to reconcile with a purely synaptic-weight framework.

items.text: Candidate answer: neural oscillations
items.detail: Oscillations segregate spiking into phases, route information locally, and open timing windows for long-range communication.

items.text: Ephaptic coupling: fields shift spiking without synapses
items.detail: Extracellular electric fields can directly nudge nearby neurons' membrane potential, synchronizing them even when synapses are blocked.

items.text: Fields spread wider, act continuously, near-instantly
items.detail: Unlike sparse, brief spikes limited by axon conduction, fields cover millimeters at once and change almost at the speed of light.

items.text: So oscillatory fields suit rapid, large-scale control
items.detail: These properties make brain waves good candidates for aligning spike timing and flexibly routing information across overlapping networks.

scenes.caption: A funnel: the failure of fixed-function neurons, the discovery of multifunctional ones, and the resulting need for a routing system, narrowing down onto oscillations and ephaptic coupling as the answer.

scenes.title: Spatial Computing, traveling waves, analog computation

items.text: Gamma excites; alpha/beta brakes, like in motor cortex
items.detail: Beta acts as a brake on movement; when it drops locally, gamma and spiking rise and movement becomes likely.

items.text: Alpha/beta act as inhibitory 'stencils' over cortex
items.detail: Alpha/beta rhythms suppress gamma and spiking in targeted spots, letting feedforward signals emerge only where alpha/beta is weak.

items.text: Confirmed in monkey PFC: patterns predict errors
items.detail: Alpha/beta rhythms carried learned contextual information in spatial patterns that mirrored sensory spiking and predicted mistakes.

items.text: Alpha/beta's millimeter scale suits top-down control
items.detail: Wave spatial reach tracks frequency: gamma is too fine-grained, slow waves too broad; alpha/beta sits at just the right scale.

items.text: This explains mixed selectivity, no 'context neuron' needed
items.detail: A neuron falls inside the stencil in one context and outside it in another, making its apparent selectivity context-dependent.

items.text: And explains low-dimensional 'subspace' coding
items.detail: Stencils segregate spiking into overlapping, structured subsets of neurons, which looks like organizing activity into separate subspaces.

items.text: Traveling waves move the stencil across cortex
items.detail: Alpha/beta patterns do not just sit still; they sweep across the cortical surface as organized traveling waves.

items.text: Moving stencils may drive shifts between coding states
items.detail: As a wave moves, it can transition population activity from one orthogonal coding subspace to another.

items.text: Wave interference performs analog computation directly
items.detail: When waves meet they add, cancel, or form new patterns through superposition, solving problems the way physical wave physics works.

items.text: This is parallel and far more energy-efficient
items.detail: An analog medium evolves all at once rather than looping through variables one at a time, which also saves energy.

scenes.caption: A chain within a chain: the stencil mechanism is proposed, confirmed, and shown to explain two puzzles, then extended in time (traveling waves) and generalized into a computing principle (wave interference).
